explanation: Mixture. Strongest repeated case is the opening '[' of an Objective-C message send right after '=' or 'return' (e.g. '= [NSOperationQueue new', 'return [CAEAGL'). Other top hits are unrelated tokens: ' Chairman', ' out' in 'throw out', 'al' in Hungarian 'azzal', 'es' in 'Memes', ' crystal' in 'liquid crystal'.

Mixture with a few small clusters: 'ogenic' in '(non)pathogenic'; ' the' right after 'save/saved' ('save the dates', 'God Save the'); ' of' in 'Democratic Republic of'; digits inside RFC/ISO standard numbers; comparatives like 'slower/slowed/rather'. No single shared feature.

Fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly in first-person technical Q&A prose ('to use [it]', 'am [not] sure', 'make the same [request]'), plus a few odd tokens like '.y' in IP ranges or digits. I can't find a clear lexical or semantic trigger.

Mixture: ' Summer' in '<year> Summer Olympics'; ' ins' in 'topological insulators'; '[' in shell 'if [ ! -f'; CSS punctuation; digits in OID strings. These are fixed, predictable continuations, but the clusters are unrelated.

Fires on a token that ends a code line with a newline right after an opening bracket, parenthesis or brace, or a trailing comma or operator, i.e. a line break inside an unfinished multi-line expression ('[
', '(
', '{
', ',
', ' &&
'). Plain sentence-final '.
' in prose fires only weakly.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word the tokenizer splits into several pieces, usually a space-led fragment such as ' Pel'(áez), ' ac'(usada), ' conf'(ederates), ' ne'(oplasm), ' Bre'(uninger). Rare or foreign words and names count most. Whole-word tokens fire weakly or not at all.

Mixture. Many hits are word-final or word-internal pieces of drug and biochemistry names ('Methad[one]', 'separ[in]', 'op[iod]', 'tachy[kin]', 'antitryps[in]'). Others are unrelated: 'for that [matter]', 'much to [say]', ' debt', '.cookie', 'Overflow'.

Fires on assorted function words and modifiers in expository prose ('barring [from]', 'harm to [other] people', 'satisfaction [is]', '[future] seasons', '[another] flower'), loosely when an object or complement is coming. Also fires on unrelated punctuation and math tokens. No clear common trigger.

Loose mixture. Some finance and economics contexts ('decline at [a] rate', 'High [Interest]', 'stock [closed]', 'below [the] median forecast'). Year digits like '2[0]08' and '2[0].04'. First pieces of names (' Hok', ' Spe', ' Li', 'Bi', 'We'). No unifying rule.

Often fires on a content verb or verb stem right after an auxiliary, negation or infinitive marker ('but [grew]', 'did not [listen]', 'haven't [posted]', 'has [published]', 'shoulder to [cry]'). Also fires on fixed phrases like 'within [walking] distance' and 'the [content] of which is incorporated', and on unrelated word pieces.

Mixture. Second halves of fixed names ('New [Zealand]', 'jsfiddle[.net]', 'Pattern [Lab]'), digits inside years, dates or IDs, and assorted words ('[September]', ' Extract', ' Human'). No clear shared feature.

Reflexive marking. Strongest on the Romance reflexive pronoun 'se'/'s'' (Portuguese, Spanish, French) and on English 'self' as a compound prefix ('self-titled', 'self-hosted', 'self-identifies'). Moderate on Python 'self' parameters. Weak on English '-self' pronouns and 'own'.

Fires on 'then' (or Russian 'то') that opens the main clause after a conditional 'if' clause, especially right after the comma. Sentence-initial 'Then' used for sequence fires only moderately, and other tokens barely at all.

Mixture: ' D' in diopters, '.read' in code, 'RICT' in 'DISTRICT', '0' in '#sec0', 'Photo' in 'AP Photo', plus assorted words from medical and science prose. Mostly predictable word endings or continuations, but no shared concept.

Fires on the word 'sleep' and its forms ('sleeping', 'sleeps', 'asleep', 'sleepiness'), in human, animal or programming senses (thread sleep, sleep_on). Related mental-state verbs like 'dreaming' and 'think' fire weakly to moderately.

Mixture with no clear trigger: '198[4]' in the Orwell title, 'BM[J]', ' sir', '.com' in URLs, '0' in CSS 'px' values, ' bypass' in 'coronary artery bypass', and others. Many are predictable completions, but they share no concept.

Fires on apostrophes that are mis-encoded or escaped inside contractions or possessives: '""' in wouldn""t, '\'' in Parkinson\'s, '' in tonight''s, ʹ, an empty token, '''. Weaker on other odd typographic separators (en dash, middle dot, \cdot, spaced punctuation).

Fires at the boundary right after a document's header or preamble: the newline after a copyright, license or '# coding=utf-8' line, 'package'/'namespace' after a license block, and newlines after US court-of-appeals headers. Also fires on generated math Q&A separators. The shared idea is the switch from boilerplate header to body.

Fires on control-flow and statement keywords and line breaks in procedural or scripting code (Pascal/Delphi, SQL, VB, Lua), shown inside Q&A posts: 'to' in 'for i=2 to n', newline after 'then'/'else', 'end;', 'RETURN', 'DECLARE', 'PUBLIC', 'if'. Weakly on other code punctuation.

Clearest pattern is the last digit of a year in copyright headers ('Copyright (c) 201[2]'). The rest is a mixture of unrelated tokens: 'VPS', 'il' in alkaliphilic, 'W' in wattage, ' of', ' survive', ' solar'.

Strongly fires on ' No' in the patent citation 'U.S. Pat. No.'. Also fires on mid-word subword pieces of foreign or rare words and names ('rem[uner]atório', 'd[\'H]istoire', '[Hy]giene', 'TEX[AS]') and on a few other tokens. The patent case is the only clean cluster.
